newsitem.title: USA: Dollar near fresh peak vs Swissy in late U.S. flow.
newsitem.headline: Dollar near fresh peak vs Swissy in late U.S. flow.

text.p: The dollar lingered near a new 21-month high versus the Swiss franc in late, pre-weekend trading amid expectations for continued low interest rates and a sluggish economy in Switzerland, experts said.

"(The Swiss) need the currency weaker to stimulate their economy," said David Ethridge, director of currency analysis in North America at MMS International. "Unless there's some surprising news, people are going to remain short Swiss."
At 1400 EST/1900 GMT, the dollar stood at 1.3050/60 Swiss francs, up from 1.2983/93 francs at the open, and just shy of the 21-month high at 1.3068 francs reached in early afternoon.
David Gilmore, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics, also tied Swiss franc weakness to the recent strength in European bond markets.

"There's been a significant bond market rally in Europe in the last two days and the Swiss is today, I think, becoming a funding currency," he said. "And that's why you're seeing some decent weakness there."
Other European currencies weakened versus the greenback.
The dollar was at 5.2285/28 French francs at 1400 EST/1900 GMT, up from 5.2155/75 francs at the open, and just below a new six-month high of 5.2310 also hit on Friday.
The dollar gained against the German unit, climbing to 1.5387/92 marks at 1400 EST/1900 GMT from 1.5350/60 marks at the open.

Gilmore said countries that are serious contenders for European Monetary Union want to see their exports supported by dollar strength. "They feel they can export more into the U.S. and help with their recovery," he added.

In a statement issued Friday, Bank of France Governor Jean-Claude Trichet said nothing could justify a depreciation of the franc versus the most credible European currencies, but he failed to mention the dollar exchange rate.
Trichet also said the nine-member Bank of France policy council has only one voice, the governor's, and any other members speak in a personal capacity.

In an interview in Le Monde on Thursday, council member Jean-Pierre Gerard said former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing was right to start a debate on the franc-mark rate when he called last week for a sharp depreciation in the French currency.
While the current franc-mark rate posed no problems, disagreement with Germany over monetary and exchange rate policy may make a change in the parity necessary, Gerard said.
Gilmore said Trichet's remarks on Friday were an effort to "set the record straight" that Gerard's comments were not the view of the central bank.

Trading wound down early on Friday as IMM currency futures ended at 1300 EST/1800 GMT one day after the Thanksgiving holiday. Some experts wondered whether the dollar could hold on to Friday's gains when trading resumed on Monday.
"Usually after a holidy traders will come in and try to get (the dollar) down to the levels where it was prior to the holiday," said Chris Adair, an assistant vice president at Mellon Bank N.A.
"So, we need to wait and see on Monday if we're higher or not," Adair said.
Elsewhere, the dollar stood at 113.80/90 yen at 1400 EST/1900 GMT, slightly above 113.70/80 yen at the open.
Sterling was barely lower at $1.6810/20 compared with $1.6815/25 at the open.
The dollar rose to Canadian $1.3506/11 from C$1.3474/79.
The Australian dollar traded around $0.8162/72 shortly after 1400 EST/1900 GMT, up from $0.8114/19 at the open.
-- Donna Sells 212 859-1668
